author.name: Frances Hodgson Burnett
author.biography: Born in Manchester, she moved with her family to Tennessee at fifteen, and also wrote Little Lord Fauntleroy and A Little Princess.

hook.text: What could bring a locked garden, and a lonely child, back to life?

paragraphs: Mary Lennox is about nine, thin, sour and used to being obeyed by servants in India. When cholera leaves her an orphan, she is sent to England to live with an uncle she has never met, at Misselthwaite Manor, an old house on the edge of the Yorkshire moor with nearly a hundred rooms, most of them locked.

Nobody there has much time for her. Her uncle is mostly away and does not want to see her, and the gardens are bare in the winter wind. But Martha, the young Yorkshire maid, talks to her as no servant ever has, and tells her about a garden that has been shut up for ten years, its door hidden and its key buried.

Mary starts to look for the garden, with help from a gruff old gardener and a robin. She also hears crying at night somewhere in the house, and nobody will tell her where it comes from. Martha's brother Dickon, a moor boy who can charm wild animals, becomes the first friend she has ever had.
Frances Hodgson Burnett wrote about bad tempers and unhappy children getting better through fresh air, work and watching things grow. Read it for Mary's slow change as much as for the garden's.

orientation.text: Twenty-seven chapters, told from close beside Mary for most of the book. Some characters speak Yorkshire, and this edition keeps a few of their words, such as wick, meaning alive.
